cells: Ice freezes into cracks and pulls rock fragments.

blocks.content: Glaciers erode the landscape through two primary mechanisms: plucking, where ice pulls away fractured rock fragments, and abrasion, where embedded debris scours the bedrock.

rows: Meltwater freezes in joints; moving ice lifts and removes rock blocks
Embedded rock debris grinds, scratches, and sands bedrock
Jointed, fractured rock and subglacial freeze-thaw cycles
Presence of basal rock fragments acting as abrasive agents
Produces steep, rugged, and jagged bedrock topography
Produces smooth, polished surfaces and linear glacial striations

items: U-shaped valleys and hanging valleys are characteristic features of glacial erosion, whereas V-shaped valleys are formed by river (fluvial) erosion.
Aretes are razor-sharp ridges formed when two adjacent cirques erode backward toward each other; three or more cirques forming a central peak create a pyramidal horn.
Fiords are glaciated valleys that have been submerged by sea water, creating deep, steep-walled coastal inlets.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Glacial erosion primarily operates through two distinct mechanisms: plucking (quarrying) and abrasion.
Plucking occurs when meltwater freezes into bedrock fractures, allowing moving ice to lift and detach shattered blocks.
Abrasion acts like sandpaper, where rock fragments embedded in the glacier's base scour, scratch, and polish the underlying bedrock.
Cirques are steep-sided, amphitheatre-shaped depressions carved out at the head of mountain glaciers.
Hanging valleys are created when smaller tributary glaciers erode less deeply than the main trunk glacier, leaving high-level valley junctions upon ice retreat.
